'American Psycho' is slick, sleek and empty, a one-joke show that drowns its message, such as it is, in red sauce and fake emotion.
Still, the result is oddly evanescent, so sleek and gym-toned that any real stab at meaning or consequence slides off and away.

'American Psycho' creates another sub-genre - ersatz horror - an odd variation that fails to tingle your spine with its copious bloodletting or titillate you via the writhing bodies in its mechanical sex scenes (complete with pornographic video illustrations).
If only the creators of this ultimate "why" musical had paid any attention to the possibilities of that kind of subtlety, they might have come up with a bearable if not a justifiable evening.

Or to put it another way: What might have sounded on paper like an ill-advised stunt — "Let's make a show about a man losing his bearings and slaughtering dozens of people!" — ends up being the timeliest, most trenchant show of the season.
If you can resign yourself to the story’s innate ambiguity, you’re in for a perversely enjoyable experience.
As a result, the final on-stage American Psycho minutes do nothing to sustain a venture that has already overstayed its welcome.
